analysis.body: {"transcript": {"text": "Dicus against S.H. Cress Company. Mrs. Peale, you may proceed whenever you're ready. Mr. Chief Justice, if it please the court. The case before you today presents three important issues for decision. The first is whether a person who entered a Cress restaurant lunch counter in 1964, August 14th, in Hattiesburg, Mississippi, whether she was deprived of her privileges and immunities as a citizen under 1983 of the United States Code Section 42 as the result of the action of law or the action of custom and usage. Now, this case is interesting because it was a waitress who put the gloss on the situation and on the Civil Rights Act of 1964 when she said to the petitioner when she went in accompanied by six black children to this restaurant, we have to serve the colored, but we don't have to serve the whites who come in with them. Now, it's this gloss that your honors have before you of this waitress in Mississippi that was affirmed by the district court below and also by the Court of Appeals. Does the record show whether this was chief and some of the management or is she reported to act under instructions? The record does so show. Does show? Yes. In fact, there are two parts of the record. One is a deposition record which becomes relevant on the second issue, which I'm just about to describe. And then the other is the record of the trial, which only goes as far as the plaintiff's case because at the end of the plaintiff's case, the district court granted a directed verdict. Now, the second important issue is whether or not the trial court was justified in granting a summary judgment against a cause of action charging that the respondent conspired with the Hattiesburg Police Department in this action of depriving the petitioner of service. And then later securing the arrest of the petitioner for vagrancy. And on the instant, she left the Crest store. Now, previous to the petitioner and these six children going into the Crest store in Hattiesburg in 1964, they had all been to the Hattiesburg Public Library. And there they asked to use the services of the library. And they were told that they were not permitted to use those services. The chief of police was called. They were asked to leave the library. And the library was closed. The third issue before your honors this morning is whether or not the Civil Rights Act of 1875, declared unconstitutional by this court in 1883 by the civil rights cases, should not be revived, and whether under these circumstances the petitioner had a right to ask for $500 statutory damages for her deprivation of the full enjoyment of the privileges of an inn or another place of public amusement. Those are the three questions which I propose to discuss this morning. Now, as to the first issue, Judge Bonsall, the district court judge, in a preliminary ruling, hobbled the entire case by the ruling as follows. He said that the plaintiff, that the petitioner in this case, would have to prove at trial that there was a custom in Mississippi of not serving white persons when serving Negroes. He then said that that custom would have to be shown at trial to be enforced by the state, and he said pursuant to the provisions of a Mississippi Code section 2056.5, which was passed in 1956, two years after the Brown decision, which said that a proprietor may choose the customers he wishes and that if the customer, having been asked to leave, if he, not having chosen him, refuses to leave, a trespass, a criminal action for trespass will lie against him. Now, he also said, but this is not too relevant here, that we would have to show that the proprietor knew of this section of the law in order to make out a case. Now, this ruling ignored the clear state of Mississippi law at that time. It ignored the fact that following the Brown decision, Mississippi passed a number of laws. It had a resolution of interposition in which it called upon all of the agencies of the government to regard the law stated by this court in the Brown decisions of 1954 to be inapplicable to the state of Mississippi. In 1954, it passed a conspiracy law which said that it would be a crime to violate the segregation laws of the state of Mississippi. In 1956, it also passed a law, 44,000 and something, which required the executive branch of the government to enforce the segregation laws of the state of Mississippi. It also passed at that time the trespass law I've just described. But Judge Bonsall did not think that this expression of the state legislative policy of Mississippi was relevant to this case, nor did the court below, which dismissed all the other legislative actions of the state of Mississippi, as having to do with school desegregation, despite the clear language of the Mississippi statutes which speak of segregation in all public places to be the policy of the state of Mississippi. The other aspect of Judge Bonsall's error was that he read into the language of 1983, which clearly states in the alternative that every person who denies a person the privileges and immunities of citizenship under color of statute, regulation, ordinance, custom, or usage is liable to that person for damages or other appropriate relief. Judge Bonsall said that the custom or usage has to be enforced by the state. Now, in this case, we submit that there was both. There was both the state action and there was the custom and usage. But the custom was not the custom of not serving white persons when you consented to serve Negroes, but it was a custom against the mixing of the races in public places. And to look at it any other way almost makes an absurdity. As pointed out quite eloquently in Judge Waterman's dissent, it would be impossible to show a long-standing policy of serving Negroes and not serving the whites that accompanied them in a state that did not serve Negroes except separately. Starting back with the decision of this court in Plessy against Ferguson, we have the statement of that custom as acceptable as the law of the land and that this court stated it, the South and sometimes the North have followed that custom for many years and it was only in 1954 when this court spoke out and said that that custom was no longer acceptable that changes commenced. I shouldn't say that changes have always been going on but that we really had the law of the land changed. The custom was testified to by the plaintiff at the trial. there was evidence in the trial record that the custom of the mixing of the races was not acceptable in Hattiesburg, Mississippi. Moreover, this custom was vividly described by the Fifth Circuit in a case called United States against the City of Jackson one year before this incident when the court said, we again take judicial notice that the state of Mississippi has a steel-hard, inflexible, undeviating official policy of segregation. The policy is stated in its laws. It is rooted in custom. The Jackson police add muscle, bone, and sinew. What's that quotation? That's from a case called United States against City of Jackson decided by the Fifth Circuit in 1963. It's not mentioned in my brief. What is the citation? Glad you asked that. One minute. 318 fed second page one. page one. And I believe you'll find that quotation on page five and six. What kind of case was that? A restaurant case? It was a case where the United States sued to enjoy segregated signs in bus centers. Restaurant? In public, I think it was in a bus station actually. And so I left out some language about the signs in the bus stations established the policy and then it was the police action enforcing it. What happened after the episode arrest of the service? Well, you see, they come from the library where the library's been closed and they've been thrown out. They go to Woolworth's first and then they go into Crest and then this happens. And the minute that she came out of the Crest door, a policeman who had been in the Crest door arrested her for vagrancy. You say they came to Crest from Woolworth's? No, well, the group had gone, it was lunchtime. They left the library, they had walked down the street of Hattiesburg and they had gone into Woolworth's. Both of these stores were... Did they eat at Woolworth's? No, it was crowded and they left Woolworth's and went into Crest. Both of these stores were supposed to be following the Civil Rights Act of 1964 and they thought they would get service at the lunch counters. The Woolworth's store was crowded so they went to the Crest store. But she was arrested immediately afterwards. Does the record show anything as to the practice of policy at Crest stores and other sections of the country? There is nothing in the record as to that except that there is a policy statement in the affidavit presented on the motion for summary judgment. There is a policy statement of Crest which you will find in the appendix which interestingly enough says that as it is written as of July 15th already 13 days after the Civil Rights Act went into effect and it says you will no longer segregate your facilities and then it says and you must stop having segregated washrooms and segregated drinking fountains and you must look and take down any signs that are still there with regard to the segregation of the races. However, and this is a footnote, one of the things that we saw in our preliminary discovery proceedings was whether or not on August 14th 1964 there were segregated facilities in the store and the district court held this was irrelevant and we were never permitted to that you will find in the appendix to my reply brief holding of the district court that it was irrelevant whether the facilities were segregated on August 14th 1964. Does that answer your question? Ms. Peel, I can't find that case in your brief. Can you give me this page again? The one in the Mississippi case? The Fifth Circuit? It isn't in my brief. I just found it. Oh, I see. But the citation is 318, Fed Second, page 1. 318, Fed Second, page 1. Now the second point of error was the granting of a summary judgment against the plaintiff before trial on the grounds that there was no justiciable, there was no triable issue on the conspiracy charge. Now, as to that, I have to be a little more technical. Justice Marshall in a recent case has set down at length when a summary judgment is appropriate appropriate, and I believe that this case is an outstanding example of when a summary judgment is not appropriate. The charge in the plaintiff's complaint was that there was a conspiracy between the officials of the police department of the city of Hattiesburg and Cress. In support of the motion for summary judgment, the respondent brought in certain affidavits, brought in one by the police commissioner, which reminds me of the old law school saying of what is a negative pregnant because he does not deny that the police had nothing to do with Cress's conduct. He says quite specifically he didn't talk to Mr. Powell, the manager, about Ms. Attick's arrest. Mr. Powell furnishes evidence in his deposition which I think suggests the conspiracy. In fact, it suggests a whole line of thought. He says that after the passage of the civil rights bill and the things that were going on in Hattiesburg, he thought a lot about people coming into Cress in mixed groups. And he decided he was going to have a policy. And that policy was going to be under certain circumstances not to serve the white person in the group. Now I submit this policy could well be one that was discussed and worked out with the police department of the city of Hattiesburg. You say could well be. Of course, that's a difficult standard on which to find facts, isn't it? Yes, but we are not finding them. We are talking about whether or not the respondent presented us with enough facts for a prima facie case. Whether we have a genuine issue of fact, that's the test, isn't it? And the genuine issue of fact arises here out of the circumstances, just as they are set forth. The police has an active role in this library refusal. The police arrest her immediately after she has been deprived of service in this restaurant. The policeman goes into the restaurant. the manager explains that he communicates with people by eye signals. The signal that he gave this time to stop the service of the petitioner was an eye signal. There is testimony that the policeman went into the store and there was an eye signal between him and one of the waitresses. Now, you can say that that's not conclusive proof, but we have a right to go to trial on these issues. We have a right to draw whatever comfort that we can from the inferences that come out of this situation. And finally, there are two things. We have a Fifth Circuit finding. Now, this is another point. This case went up to the Fifth Circuit, a case involving the same facts, but it went up on a removal petition of this petitioner and four other petitioners who were arrested for vagrancy in the library on the following Monday, August 17th. And these cases were removed, the criminal cases, the vagrancy cases, were removed to the federal court under Judiciary Code Section 1443. the District Court remanded these cases to the state court. They were appealed to the Fifth Circuit. And the Fifth Circuit made a finding, a fact, that Ms. Addix was arrested for attempting to enjoy equal public accommodations in the Hattiesburg Public Library and a restaurant in a nationally known Cress store. That is a finding of fact. Had the District Court found that fact first? The District Court did not find that fact. The Fifth Circuit found it as a matter of law with regard to the state of the record as it arrived before it. The District Court permitted the filing of a series of affidavits which were not controverted with regard to the conduct of the petitioners. the Circuit Court found as a matter of fact that there was proof. And you'll find that decision in 393 Fed Second. That is in my brief. What was the page on that again? Well, we'll check it if it's in your brief. It is in my brief. You won't need to give it to us now. You may go right on with your arm. 468. Then finally, and I don't think this is an unimportant aspect of the conspiracy case, I submit to your honors that the custom of segregation shared and supported by the police, the custom in Hattiesburg, where it was supported by private persons, represented a conspiracy between the law enforcement officers and the private persons enforcing the doctrine of segregation. And the facts here show that that is what was happening and that's what occurred in this case. That you have a, besides an express conspiracy, you have a silent conspiracy which you can look for the support to of the events as they occurred. Of course, if you prevail on the first branch of your case, the conspiracy of the matter is quite unimportant to you. Did you say it was unimportant to me? Yes, if you prevail on the first branch of your case, this was done, absolute conspiracy, under color of law, under color of custody. But you put the arms as king. Sure, surely, surely. Irrespective of the conspiracy. Yes, but I have a stronger case with the conspiracy. You see, in bringing this case before a jury and in bringing all the facts before a jury, one is foreclosed from bringing out the facts of the arrest. And one is, we weren't foreclosed from bringing out the facts of the incident in the library, but it becomes a much stronger, a much more compelling case before a jury if one can show the whole story. Actually, a jury wouldn't get the whole story. That just makes your case stronger after you get back there. You don't need that second layer of strength here if you prevail as Justice Marshall's. I have to tell you I need it. Justice Harlan suggested. I need it only in the sense you need everything you want. I need it because if I go back, I want the strongest case I can get. It's true I would win if it's just scoring, but I'm saying for an effective presentation of the plaintiff's case, it is necessary to have the conspiracy count. The essence of your position is that Judge Bonsall took too narrow a view of what had to be shown as custom, I mean the color of custom. You say that it's enough to show a policy of segregation as distinguished from pinpointing the custom of refusing to serve whites in the company of blacks. Exactly. That's the essence of your position. Exactly. Exactly. Would the proprietor have violated any Mississippi law if he had served whites and Negroes together? Well, if he had talked about it before, he would have violated the misdemeanor section which is 2056 subdivision 7 of conspiring to overthrow the segregation laws the way that was formed. But what if he had just refused to, had just gone ahead and served this group at this table? Well, he was under, he was under orders by the Federal Civil Rights Act to do that, but he didn't. What do you mean with him? Well, that is my question. I asked would he violate any Mississippi law. I say, that conspiracy law. If he talked about it, if he talked about it with someone else. But if he didn't, what if he didn't? If he didn't talk about it with anyone else, I suppose... Well, what law, what if he had talked about it? If he talked about it with someone else, he would, that could be a conspiracy. What law would he have been conspiring to overthrow? The segregation law. Because that's violating the segregation law to serve somebody a public... Well, is there a segregation law in Mississippi forbidding the serving of the two races in a restaurant? Well, that's the way the statute 2056, parenthesis 7, end, paren says. Well, that's it. That's just a trespass law. No, no, no. That's another one. What does it say? 2046.5. What does this segregation law say for a restaurant? It's not for restaurants. It's a general law. It's 2056, subdivision 7. If two or more persons conspire to overthrow or violate the segregation laws of this state through force, violence, threats, intimidation, or otherwise... Well, yes, conspire to overthrow the segregation laws, but what segregation laws? Well, I suppose... Is there a segregation law against serving whites and Negroes together in a restaurant? Or even serving Negroes in a restaurant? Well, I can only refer you to what the Fifth Circuit said, that there is such a law in Mississippi, and it's enforced by law, and it's enforced by custom. Well, can you find in the statute? I think I have. Well, you just say that the law says you can't conspire to overthrow the segregation laws, and I just want to know what the segregation laws are that you're conspiring to overthrow. Well, I think that perhaps part of the vagueness of it has to do with the Mississippi position on it. Everybody in Mississippi knows what they are. There is no specific Mississippi statute that says it's unlawful to serve whites and Negroes together in a restaurant. There's none that I know of that says just that, but I think that the sum total of the laws that I've cited suggest that there is law which disapproves of that kind of conduct. Now, we also get into the right Whitman against Mulkey situation or Hunter against Erickson where you have no law in the state before the Brown decision. You're supposed to have the common law. Then, after the Brown decision, the trespass statute is passed which says that a proprietor may choose his customers and refuse service to anyone he chooses. And if the person to whom he's refused service refuses to leave, he can be charged with trespass. Now, there you have still an answer to your question because there you have affirmative state action, at least cutting down on what would otherwise be the common law rule. And I am now going to take issue with the Williams-Hot shop statement of what the common law was in Virginia and state that my understanding of the common law in the southern states at the time of the passage of the 14th amendment is that an in or other victualer, which means a restaurant, has an obligation to serve all persons who come in. And that is an interpretation that is found in the old common law and which former Justice Goldberg, in a concurring opinion in Bell against Maryland, also cited in my brief, says, must have been the understanding of the framers of the 14th amendment and of the framers of the reconstruction statutes at the time they were passed. Mr. Field, you're impinging on your rebuttal time if you want to save any. You're almost out of time, if not out. All right, well, I will... I think you have only one minute left. All right, well, I will... If you want to save it for rebuttal. I may not. I want to talk a bit about the 1875 statute and about breathing life into the old civil rights statute in line with the same thing I was talking about. It seems to me that in Jones against Meyer, this court through Mr. Justice Stewart set the basis for a new line of thinking and that is finding support and authority for the implementation of federal law on the discrimination as to private rights in the 13th amendment. amendment. And it seems to me that the 13th amendment plus the commerce clause very clearly reactivate and revive the act of 1875. Now, I'm going to ask your honors, and I'm through, I'm going to ask your honors to consider this in the line of what Mr. Justice Stewart said there with regard to the distinctions made by the respondent and the courts below, that there is no place in the jurisprudence of a nation of this kind of thinking where we are trying, striving to join the human race. Mr. Littock. Mr. Chief Justice, may it please the court. This, as the court knows, was a civil action brought against S.H. Crescent Company in the Southern District of New York seeking damages against Crescent in excess of a half million dollars for an alleged violation of Section 1983 of Title 42. Crescent prevailed in the District Court and was affirmed in the Court of Appeals of the Second Circuit. The facts are very simple and in the main are not in dispute. On August 14, 1964, the plaintiff, a white New York City school teacher, was in Hattiesburg, Mississippi, came into Hattiesburg with a group of six Negro students in an effort to integrate the library. Having been refused the library services, the students and the group left, went to Woolworths, which they found to be crowded, came to Crescent, where a waitress, acting under the directions of the store manager, offered to take the orders of the Negro students, but declined to take that of plaintiff. The group thereupon got up and left, and subsequent to that, the plaintiff was arrested on the streets of Hattiesburg. Petitioner alleged a conspiracy in the district court below, charging that Crescent had conspired with the police to do three things, one, to deny the library services, two, to have her arrested, and three, to have her refuse service. After the complaint was filed, your honors, a year of discovery took place. Depositions were had on both sides. interrogatories were served by both sides. Documents were produced by the plaintiff to the defendant and by the defendant to the plaintiff. After a year, a note of issue was filed, telling the court that all discovery was completed, both sides were satisfied, and the case was in all respects ready for trial. Then and only then, did Crescent move for summary judgment. Crescent moved for summary judgment on a conspiracy claim on the grounds that the record clearly showed there were no genuine material issues of fact for trial. Plaintiff, in rebutting or attempting to rebut that case, that claim, sought to rely, and still does according to her brief, on the mere sequence of events as alleged in the complaint. We contend that the record made it clear that whatever conjecture may have existed at the time of the complaint, it had been dispelled by discovery. The library incident, for example, is probably the most far-fetched of the three. The plaintiff testified that she and the Negro students came into town on August 14, 1964, having told no one that they were coming. No one at Crescent certainly knew. They went to the library, where a librarian whose name is not known to them and not known to Crescent, called the police, it seems, and refused them service. We questioned the plaintiff, and we said, was there any mention of Crescent at this time? This is not a suit against the police or the library? And the answer was no. And we said, well, do you have any proof, any rumor, any hearsay, anything that ties Crescent to the library? And the answer was no. And we took the deposition, or rather the plaintiff did, of Mr. Powell, our store manager, and said, did you ever talk to anyone about the library incident? And he said, no. And they asked him, when did you first find out about it? And he said, when I went home that night and read about it in the newspaper. Now the group left the library, the police closed it, and they walked to the Woolworths store. They decided to go get lunch. Obviously no one knew that either. But the plaintiff testified that the police followed her, that she saw police all around her. Now Crescent couldn't have called those police and didn't. It didn't even know she was in town. She went to the Woolworths store, which was crowded, came out, and saw a policeman in front of the store, in front of Woolworths. They decided on the spur of the moment to go to Crescent. And why did they decide to go to Crescent? They decided to go to Crescent because Crescent had integrated its facilities. It had one set of facilities at which both blacks and whites were served. This is clear in the record. Plaintiff's own witnesses testified to this. There can be no dispute about that. The very witnesses she called upon the trial had eaten at these facilities at the same time white people ate of them. There were only one set of facilities. Now as they came to the Crescent store, they noticed the police car parked out in front. Again, the same police, whatever the police may have done, Crescent didn't call them. Crescent didn't even know they were there. She sat down in the booth. And it is true, we admit, that the store manager determined not to serve Miss Addicts while offering service to the Negroes in the group. He candidly stated on deposition when asked why he did that, that Crescent had a policy, and I don't think it's a policy, it's a policy which is printed, and it says it is now the law and company policy to serve everyone without regard to race, color, or greed. And he said, I had served Negroes at my facility along with whites. I had served them when they came in together, jointly. I served them, indeed, on the day in question, and on every day since then. He said, I declined to serve Miss Addicts for one reason and one reason only. When she came in and I looked outside, and I saw the crowd that was out there, and I heard the milling that was in my store, I feared that there was going to be a riot. I feared that there would have been violence directed to her, which would have led to a situation where we could have never served again. We would have closed the lunch counter, for good. And that I didn't think would accomplish anything. Now, the plaintiff got up and left the store. It wasn't asked to, but did, having been declined service. Thereafter, it appears she was arrested by the police. Now, we again asked the plaintiff, did the police ever mention Crest to you? Do you have any facts you rely upon? Her answer was no. We said, well, is there anything you can point to? Her answer was no. We took the deposition of Mr. Powell, the plaintiff did, and he categorically stated, categorically, that he had no communication with any police official, at any time, about Ms. Attucks or any civil rights worker. What was the ground for the arrest? It appears the ground for the arrest was vagrancy, a charge of loitering on the public streets of Hattiesburg. Now, however valid or invalid or trumped up that charge may have been, it had nothing to do with Crest. Mr. Powell testified he didn't know about it until he read it in the papers the next time. How long after the petitioner left your client's door was she arrested? It appears minutes after that the police car that she had seen across the street when she came over swung across and arrested her. Now, the police, now, Mr. Powell said I never communicated with the police. I didn't even know about it until that night. Did that arrest lead to a trial and conviction? No, Your Honor, as I understand it, what happened was that the plaintiff filed a petition for removal of that arrest to the federal court. That's the Aktenberg case that came up to the court of appeals. I might quickly tell the court that for this petitioner to rely upon that case and some support in this case is really unwarranted. The fact is, twofold, one, that in the Aktenberg case, as the court of appeals note, there was no trial. It was an uncontested issue. Plaintiffs put in affidavits. The police never showed up in the years, never rebutted this, and it went up on an uncontested record, and the city of Hattiesburg didn't even bother to file a brief it appears in the court of appeals. Moreover, of course, Kress was not a party to that case. We didn't even know about it. We didn't go in and cross-examine. We'll find out. You see, the court there said that the arrest was related to her activities in Kress, which may be true. Maybe that's why the police did arrest her. But that doesn't mean that Kress had anything to do with the arrest. That doesn't tie Kress into it, and that's, I think, the scene that went on for the conspiracy. That's the United States Court of Appeals that said that. Yes, sir. The case was, I just want to get the factual answers to my question, if I may. She was arrested a few moments after leaving the store on a charge of vagrancy. Yes, sir. When this charge was brought in the state court, a petition for removal to the United States District Court was filed. Not opposed, as I understand it. No, as I understand it, Mr. Justice Stewart, the defendant petitioned to remand to the state court. After the removal? Yes, sir. And that was denied? That was, no. I believe that was granted by the District Court. Then, the plaintiff appealed, they reversed that and said it was properly removed and the case should be dismissed. And then what happened? And the case was then dismissed? Yes, I believe. In the District Court? In the federal court? Yes, that's correct. That is correct. Was there any, does the record show there was any promotion or disturbance outside the, outside the store? There is testimony to that effect, yes, sir. The store manager testified to that. I know, but what is the fact that he testified to that there was any evidence in the district? Well, I think it's fair to say that is the only evidence in the record on the point, yes. Yes, that is the only evidence on the point. Now, we think that when we came forward with these affidavits, I might quickly say we also had affidavits from the police, which said that they had never communicated with anyone in Crest concerning this arrest, and it was an arrest that they made on their own discretion on the streets of Hattiesburg. We believe that when we came forward with this kind of proof, it was incumbent, as this court has held in the City Service case, upon the petitioner to come forth with something, something which would show an inference of conspiracy. There's a little difference between City Service. In this case, City Service was 10 or 12 years. Yes, Your Honor. This was one year. Except for the fact, Your Honor, that all discovery was completed. The plaintiff confessed she desired no more and never requested any more in the District Court. Well, I don't see why you need City Service for that. Well, what I was really trying to say is that in City Service, where the party had come forth with evidence, which the other party didn't rebut, in City Service, as Your Honor recalls, the other party, that is the plaintiff, had sought additional discovery. And one of the issues was whether the District Court properly denied it. Here, there was no such request. The additional discovery they wanted was from a dead man. I mean, I just think that case stands for its own. I understand, Your Honor. What worries me is, was there any allegation at all that this petitioner was broke? I'm sorry.
